hook_text: Your kitchen runs at 230 volts. The line over the Free State runs at 400 000. Here is why, and how it gets back down to your kettle.
clip_script: A battery gives DC, one way. A spinning generator gives AC, swinging fifty times a second. Wires waste power as heat with the square of the current, so you send power at huge volts and tiny amps. A transformer, two coils on one iron core, changes AC volts by its turns ratio: more turns, volts up; fewer, volts down; amps go the other way. Station to 400 kilovolts, pylons across the country, substations down to 132, 11, then the green box on your pavement to 230. Frequency at 50 hertz means supply equals demand; load shedding is the grid cutting some areas to keep the rest at 50.
visual_style: Whiteboard DC flat line versus AC wave; a transformer with coils of different turns; a map of South Africa with pylons, substations and voltages stepping down; a frequency meter hovering at 50.
pacing: AC versus DC, losses, transformer, grid journey, frequency.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and trace the voltages from the station to your socket.
